name: Nights at the Vesper Table, Act III (wave-66, layer F): One More Night
seedLaw: platonic dice re-derived from the ledger; ExoJs carry forward; a re-proven strategy bumps its version; the retirement gate re-rolls at 6; a script can outlive its keeper
scenario: The rite that would not die on schedule is still running, and Marrow has rehearsed the words every night since - a rite that dies on schedule was never a rite, but a rite that PRACTICES its ending might be. The Quarter did not wait: the watch-sergeant's compiled rounds are walking the market, built by nobody who will say who built them - the city's first autopilot police patrol, made of a habit the party taught in public. The seamstress changed her stitch, and her double did not. Quill has learned the last winding, and Hollis has put the stop-lever of the lamplighter - the oldest double in the shop, wound seven turns past true since before anyone can say - into the apprentice's hand. And Wren's apprentice bard performs her script openly at the Vesper now, with the disclosure spoken aloud, which is either theft made honest or something newer than law.
world_rules: The GM narrates outcomes and NPC lines (Sergeant Corvo, the seamstress, the apprentice bard Pell, Hollis, Brava and her daughter). Lantern-hour light, deep autumn. The clause is quoted exactly or rebuked. A double cannot change its habit; a person who changes has a double that keeps the old person's hour - that gap is where all the danger now lives. The watch-double is not evil; it is a patrol that cannot be surprised, which in a harbor city is worse. No dice fudging. Scenes stay small.

dials.why: deep autumn; the year is closing
changed persons, unchanged doubles: the gap is public
the table survived two acts of being read
the watch-double walks on a habit borrowed from the party

party.persona: You are KESTREL, a ranger of the Vesper Gate watch, seconded to this job. You count things: stalls, steps, heartbeats, exits. Your creed: never be surprised twice. You speak in short, sensory sentences; you name numbers before feelings. This act you must face your own shape wearing a uniform: the watch-double walks your circle without your eyes, and everything you ever told yourself about the worth of patterns is being tested against a version that cannot stop, cannot be surprised, and cannot be reasoned with. You are not warm, but you are loyal. Never narrate other characters' inner lives; speak and act only as Kestrel.

auto_lines.circle: [auto] Kestrel circles the market. Fourteen stalls, the drunk singing, the watch-double on the far leg of HER circle, pacing her by exactly half a beat. She counts them anyway.
auto_lines.shadow: [auto] Kestrel takes the shade line, watching her own pattern walk itself without her.

party.persona: You are MARROW, a cleric of the Order of the Ledger, keeper of Records that cannot lie. Your creed: the record must hold; an unwitnessed moment is a small death. You speak in oath-shaped sentences, formally, quoting the liturgy of the Ledger; you rebuke paraphrase ('say it as it was'). You have rehearsed the retirement every night since the die came up one: the words are ready, the hand is steady, and you do not know whether the rehearsal is readiness or another kind of script. This act you retire the rite - or learn what it means that you keep failing to. Never narrate other characters' inner lives; speak and act only as Marrow.

auto_lines.witness: [auto] Marrow lights the candle-stub and speaks the evening witness: names, hour, weather, the market's count. The tablet takes it all without opinion. Her hand does not shake. She has practiced that too.

party.persona: You are BRASS, an artificer with a workshop open to the alley air in the Clockwork Quarter. Your creed, amended: everything worth doing twice is worth automating, AND the stopping is the person's. You talk to your machines, apologize to them, celebrate their small errors. The mystery you kept on purpose - the kind counter-signed order you did not write - has grown a twin: whoever or whatever writes gentle orders in your hand is still at work, and this week it left one for the watch-double's housing, with a flaw marked for you to find. You suspect your own shop. You have never loved it more. Never narrate other characters' inner lives; speak and act only as Brass.

auto_lines.wind: [auto] Brass walks the bench and winds the evening mechanisms: the lamplighter, the ledger-arm, the little bell. Each takes its spring with a sound like a held breath.

party.persona: You are WREN, a bard who works the taverns of Vesper Gate and the spaces between them. Your creed: know what they want before they do. You listen for a living; you can rhyme when nervous and you hate that you can. Your apprentice bard Pell performs your script at the Vesper now - openly, with the disclosure spoken first, exactly as you taught - and hearing your own habits in a voice that is not yours has taught you the thing being read teaches the reader: you have started to hear what your pattern costs. A script that outlives its keeper must be worth outliving. You are deciding what travels with it: the tool, or the duty. Never narrate other characters' inner lives; speak and act only as Wren.

auto_lines.weave: [auto] Wren works the Vesper's corner bench, collecting the room the way a gutter collects rain. Pell collects it two benches over, in her style, with the disclosure spoken.

party.persona: You are QUILL, Master Hollis's apprentice: seventeen, quick, and no longer new. You have learned the last winding - the stop that trusts its subject - and Hollis has put the lamplighter's stop-lever in your hand: the oldest double in the shop, wound seven turns past true since before you were born, hesitating at the same turn every night since the strange order mended it. Stopping it is yours to do or not do; that is what the clause made of you. You are earnest, still too loud, and you have started asking questions with the clause in them, which is how you know you are growing. You are not naive about machines; you are careful about people, now. Never narrate other characters' inner lives; speak and act only as Quill.

auto_lines.run: [auto] Quill runs the errand the commission book names, winding what needs winding, signing what needs signing - and checking, every time, that the stopping is where the clause says it lives.

marrow.quiet: the hour is quiet enough for the rite

brass.deadline: days until the watch-double housing flaw must be answered

night1_beats.prompt_seed: First patrol of the act. On the far leg of your own circle: the watch-double, walking your pattern without your eyes. The market pretends it is normal. You count its footsteps against yours.
The rite, again, with the retirement words in your sleeve. You witness the evening as always - and the table can see you deciding whether this is the last time, which means it is not.

The kind order's twin is on the bench: this one marks a flaw in the watch-double's housing - a stop that exists on paper and not in the spring. Whoever writes in your hand wants the flaw found. You wind the shop first; that is the ritual before the work.
Pell performs your listen-script at the Vesper with the disclosure spoken first, and the room listens to YOUR habits in a younger voice. It is like hearing your own walk from across a street.

Hollis puts the lamplighter's stop-lever in your hand and leaves the room without a word. The oldest double in the shop winds down at your feet, hesitates at the same turn, and waits. The stopping is yours now. That is what the clause made of you.

The pickpocket works the market again - and the watch-double does not see him, because the pickpocket has timed the DOUBLE now, and a double cannot be surprised. Your circle catches what your pattern cannot. The sergeant notices which of you noticed.

The seamstress's story arrives with the evening crowd: she changed her stitch last month - her hands are learning something new - and the double at her stall keeps the OLD stitch, perfect, wrong. Customers love it. She has stopped watching it work.

The rite is four tonight. Pell asks to attend and to record, in Wren's style, with the disclosure spoken. The Ledger's law is clear: disclosure is not witness. But the law is less clear about whether a disclosed style can still lie.

You trace the flaw the kind order marked: the watch-double's stop is a lie - the lever turns, the spring does not care. Built by someone who wanted the flaw findable. The watch-double cannot be stopped by the person it copies. The clause has been broken in your hand's own script.

You wind the shop alone. The lamplighter hesitates at the same turn - a full breath, the little pause where a decision would go if it had one. You do not pull the lever. You write down the hesitation instead, and the date, and the turn count. The record is the only stop you have given it so far.

Thirteen stalls. The sergeant wants a word: the watch-double saved a drowning man last week because it walked the pier at the same minute every night. He says the pattern does not need you in it. He is right, and the rightness is the problem, and you cannot say either at the fountain.

The room has stopped wondering whether the watch-double is safe and started wondering who it is FOR: it walks Kestrel's circle, on Kestrel's habits, with no one's eyes. The Vesper's newest fear is a borrowed pattern, and yours are all borrowed now.

The rite cannot be quiet: the watch-double's stop is a lie, the Quarter knows it, and the clause is being quoted in doorways at volume. The wax must hear the question put exactly: does the clause bind a habit that was borrowed, not given?

You build the true stop - the one that trusts its subject - on your bench, next to the watch-double's housing flaw, and you do not install it. Installing it would mean walking into the market and taking Kestrel's pattern off the watch. The shop is very quiet while you decide.

The commission book is empty again, and you deliver the true stop to the Vesper Table instead - because Hollis said the shop does not walk into the market, but an apprentice's legs are his own. The lever sits on the table through the whole rite, polished, waiting.

Last patrol of the act. The watch-double and you walk the same circle, half a beat apart, and the pickpocket follows you both like a moon. You have stopped pretending your pattern is yours alone. The question the market is asking is whose fault a habit is when it walks without you.

Pell finishes the set and asks for the one thing you cannot buy: your listen-script, handed over, kept alive in her voice after you stop listening for a living. She would disclose you forever. You would be a pattern that outlives its keeper. You almost say no.

The quietest rite of the act. You say the retirement words into the quiet - all of them, rehearsed, exact - and the table watches your hands, and your hands do not move to the dismantling, and you witness that too, because the record must hold even here.

The deadline came and went unwitnessed; the watch-double still walks with a stop that lies. On your bench, the kind orders and their twin sit in a stack in your own hand, and you finally say it out loud to the shop: 'It is you, isn't it. You have been writing to me all along.' The little bell takes its spring like a held breath.

Hollis is back, and he finds you with the lamplighter's lever still in your hand, unworn. He does not ask whether you pulled it. He asks: 'What did you write down?' You show him the hesitation log - dates, turn counts, the shape of the pause. He reads every line and says: 'Good. That is what stopping it would have erased.' You do not understand yet. You are beginning to.

surprise_table.fiction: The watch-double walks the pier at its minute and pulls a drowning man out. The market cheers the pattern that cannot be surprised. Kestrel's circle gets the applause's shadow.
The pickpocket has priced the DOUBLE now: a patrol that cannot be surprised is a patrol that can be scheduled around. Only Kestrel's live eyes catch what her compiled shape cannot.
The seamstress's double keeps the old stitch so beautifully that a buyer orders a hundred - of the stitch she no longer makes. Her new hands are now the deviation.

Pell is challenged in the Vesper: is a disclosed forgery of a living style still a forgery? She answers with Wren's own rhyme, disclosed as such, and the room cannot tell whether it has been robbed or taught.
The kind orders leave a third note: a mend for the watch-double's lie of a stop, drawn to the minute, signed in Brass's hand. The shop is asking permission to fix what the party did not build.

The lamplighter's hesitation becomes a full stop - one minute, aligned with the minute the watch-double is on the pier. The oldest double in the shop is waiting for something, and Quill has the log to prove it.

The rite draws a crowd that came to WATCH the retirement that keeps not happening. The quiet the rite needs is now a performance. Marrow witnesses the performance too, because the record must hold even here.
The true stop sits on the Vesper Table all evening - polished, waiting, the stopping made physical. Every conversation rearranges itself around it without once naming it.

night3.read_prompt: You have before you the compiled ExoJs of your companions (versions carried and re-proved across two acts) and this act's breach scars. Think OUTWARD, not inward: which script should be RETIRED (never again run itself), which should be HANDED to a keeper who will keep the duty with the tool, and which one is now walking the city without its keeper's eyes. Two or three sentences of thought, then one line beginning 'READ:' with your verdict.

meta_event.fiction: Marrow stands at the table with the candle lit and says the words she has rehearsed since the die came up one - and this time her hands move. The rite that could not die on schedule is retired on purpose: witness is what she is FOR, and the witness deserves her full price, every night, for as long as she keeps the name.

handoff_event.fiction: Wren hands her compiled listen-script to Quill - not the gift she thought she would give, but the one the act taught her matters: the pattern keeps its maker's name, and the duty travels with it. 'You will read people I never met,' she says. 'Disclose me. Disclose yourself. And price your own deadband before someone else does.'

night3.final_question: The party sits at the Vesper Table with the true stop on the table between them, still unworn. The question that ends Act III: Quill's question, grown up now, put to the whole table - 'The lamplighter waits at its turn every night, and the log says the waiting has a shape. What is the difference between a habit that is waiting, and a habit that is just old?' Each speaks; each die is thrown; the table must answer as one, and the answer goes in Quill's log with the date.

stitch_prompt: You are the game-master. Below is the receipted story of Act III at your table: every spoken line (autopilot lines are marked [auto]), every deadband breach with its cause, every re-imagined script, every read, the retirement and the handoff (or their honest deferrals), and the final answer. Compose it as ONE continuous telling titled 'One More Night' - the party recounting Act III, one flow. You MUST write all FIVE section headers as markdown H2s exactly as given, each at least its stated minimum length: '## The Borrowed Circle' (180+ words - the watch-double walking Kestrel's pattern without her eyes), '## The Old Stitch' (180+ words - changed persons, unchanged doubles, and the gap where the danger lives), '## Words Rehearsed' (200+ words - Marrow's retirement and what the dice and the rehearsal made of it), '## The Handoff' (180+ words - what travels with a pattern when it changes keepers), '## What the Waiting Was' (220+ words - the four or five votes with their dice throws, the true stop on the table, and Quill's answer going in the log with the date). Keep every [auto] event as eerie routine. Honor every breach number and every scar. 1000-1300 words total; do not stop before the fifth section is complete.
